findings.title: Untrusted run IDs can escape the discarded directory
findings.evidence: `self.run_log.parent / "discarded" / f"{attempt.run_id or 'run'}.diff"` uses `attempt.run_id` as a path component without validation.
findings.consequence: If a worker or other caller can supply a run ID containing path separators or an absolute path, the write can escape `discarded` and truncate or create a `.diff` file elsewhere. This is a path traversal/write vulnerability.

findings.title: Attempts without unique run IDs overwrite preserved work
findings.evidence: `attempt.run_id or 'run'` gives every attempt with an empty run ID the same destination, `discarded/run.diff`.
findings.consequence: When multiple reverted attempts lack run IDs, each later write replaces the earlier saved diff; earlier receipts then point to a file containing different work, losing the recovery data this change is intended to preserve.

findings.title: Common `python -m pip` installs bypass the review rule
findings.evidence: The pip command pattern starts with `\b(?:pip3?|pipx|uv\s+pip|uv\s+tool)\s+install\b`.
findings.consequence: A command such as `python -m pip install untrusted-helper` does not match, so an agent can install a named package without this rule requesting review.

findings.title: A requirements-file option suppresses review even when the command also installs a named package
findings.evidence: The pip pattern has the negative lookahead `(?![^\n]*\s(?:-r|--requirement)\b` before matching a package name.
findings.consequence: A command such as `pip install untrusted-helper -r requirements.txt` is excluded entirely, even though it installs the named package as well as the requirements. The same can happen when another command containing `-r` follows on the same line.

findings.title: Options written with `=value` can prevent a package install from matching
findings.evidence: The option pattern is `(?:\s+-[-\w=]+)*\s+`; for example, it cannot consume `--index-url=https://...` as one option.
findings.consequence: Commands such as `pip install --index-url=https://example.invalid/simple untrusted-helper` fail to match because the pattern stops at the colon and never reaches the package name. The same issue affects options such as npm's `--registry=https://...`.

findings.title: Valid package names beginning with a digit are not detected
findings.evidence: The package-name pattern requires `[A-Za-z]` as its first character.
findings.consequence: Valid names such as `2to3` or `3to2` are not matched by `pip install 2to3` or `uv add 2to3`, so those installs avoid review.

verified.title: Common `python -m pip` installs bypass the review rule
verified.evidence: The pip command pattern starts with `\b(?:pip3?|pipx|uv\s+pip|uv\s+tool)\s+install\b`.
verified.consequence: A command such as `python -m pip install untrusted-helper` does not match, so an agent can install a named package without this rule requesting review.
verified.label: keep
verified.reason: The added pip pattern accepts `pip`/`pip3` but not `python -m pip`, so that command is not matched by this rule.

verified.consequence: A command such as `pip install untrusted-helper -r requirements.txt` is excluded entirely, even though it installs the named package as well as the requirements. The same can happen when another command containing `-r` follows on the same line.
verified.label: keep
verified.reason: The negative lookahead rejects the pip install match if any later text on the same line contains `-r` or `--requirement`, including when a named package is also installed.

findings.consequence: Commands using flags that accept URL or path values (e.g., `pip install --index-url https://pypi.org/simple requests`) will incorrectly match the URL portion as the package name. findings.title: VCS URLs (git+, hg+, svn+) match the package name pattern
findings.consequence: Direct VCS installation commands like `pip install git+https://github.com/user/repo` will match because they start with a letter and aren't blocked by the path exclusion. While VCS installs are also risky, they bypass the package index entirely, making the rule's description ('resolves to whatever the index holds under it') inaccurate for these cases.
